title: Methodological Alignment Between the EU Joint Clinical Assessment and National Health Technology Assessment Systems: A Qualitative Comparative Study of Six European Jurisdictions
content: Objectives. Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 introduces the Joint Clinical Assessment (JCA), a common descriptive clinical evaluation that Member States must take into account in national appraisal. Because national health technology assessment (HTA) systems have developed distinct methodologies, their alignment with the JCA is uncertain. We characterised it across six European jurisdictions and interpreted how the pattern arose. Methods. Qualitative comparative study combining structured expert-consensus rating with documentary process tracing. Two EU-HTA methodologists derived 35 methodological dimensions in five domains from the Regulation, its Implementing Regulation and HTA Coordination Group guidance, fixing and source-tracing the JCA reference position for each before any national rating. Expert pairs in six jurisdictions (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands and England) rated their system against every reference position by consensus, on an anchored three-point qualitative alignment scale. Reporting follows the SRQR. Results. Germany was aligned on 33 of 35 dimensions, with no substantial divergence. England was most distant (23 substantially divergent), followed by France (18); Italy and the Netherlands were intermediate (14 each). Spain recorded no aligned dimension but the fewest substantial divergences of any non-German system (7), diverging in degree rather than in kind. Divergence concentrated in the domains the JCA excludes and in appraisal posture, yet German proximity persisted once these were removed (27 of 29; 19 of 20). Documentary evidence on the legislative compromise, EUnetHTA21 methodological production and subgroup leadership suggests the JCA has emerged as a German-compatible default rather than a neutral synthesis of national traditions. Conclusions. National methodologies align with the JCA to markedly different degrees, the closest fit being the most codified national model. The alignment finding is empirical, the influence account interpretive; neither ranks any national model as superior. Because divergence concentrates where national appraisal remains sovereign, the framework may displace methodological heterogeneity downstream rather than resolve it.
